nameStory: The eastern jack-o'-lantern mushroom gets its spooky name from its brilliant orange color that glows like a carved Halloween pumpkin. Even more amazing, the gills actually glow in the dark with a greenish bioluminescent light - just like a real jack-o'-lantern! This eerie nighttime glow makes it one of the most memorable mushrooms you'll ever encounter.
description: The eastern jack-o'-lantern is a striking bright orange mushroom that grows in large clusters on decaying wood. These eye-catching fungi can form impressive bouquets of dozens of mushrooms, each with a funnel-shaped cap that can reach 4-8 inches across. The vibrant orange color ranges from deep pumpkin to golden yellow-orange, making them impossible to miss during fall woodland walks. Their most famous feature is their ability to glow in the dark with a ghostly green light.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Bright orange gills run down the stem (called decurrent) and glow with greenish bioluminescence in complete darkness - bring them into a dark room to see this magic trick

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Vibrant orange caps start convex but develop a funnel or vase shape with age, feeling smooth and slightly sticky when fresh

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in large overlapping clusters from the same base, never alone - think of orange bouquets sprouting from dead wood

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Orange stems that are often curved or off-center, feeling firm and fibrous with no ring around them

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a cream to pale yellow spore print when caps are placed gill-side down on white paper overnight

idTips.label: Safety Warning
idTips.description: POISONOUS - causes severe digestive illness and can be confused with edible oyster mushrooms. Never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification

habitat: Look for jack-o'-lanterns growing from the stumps, roots, and buried wood of deciduous trees, especially oaks and other hardwoods. They're common in mixed forests, wooded parks, and anywhere dead hardwood trees are decomposing. You'll often find them clustered around the base of dying trees or sprouting from seemingly bare ground where roots are rotting underground.

seasonality.spring: Not typically visible in spring as they fruit later in the year when conditions become right.
seasonality.summer: May begin appearing in late summer after periods of warm, humid weather and adequate rainfall.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for jack-o'-lanterns, especially September through October when they create spectacular orange displays that perfectly match autumn colors.
seasonality.winter: Usually finished fruiting by winter, though dried remnants may persist on stumps and logs.

funFact: Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms are among the few bioluminescent fungi in North America - their gills actually glow bright green in complete darkness for up to 40 hours after being picked, bright enough to read by if you have enough of them!
confusionNotes: Dangerously confused with edible oyster mushrooms, but jack-o'-lanterns have true gills (not shallow pores), grow from hardwood (not often on conifers), and always cluster from a central base. Remember: 'Oysters on logs, jack-o'-lanterns from roots and stumps.' The bioluminescent gills are the definitive test - oyster mushrooms never glow.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the spooky name and appearance, jack-o'-lantern mushrooms play an important ecological role as saprophytes, breaking down dead hardwood and recycling nutrients back to the forest. The bioluminescence may help attract insects that spread their spores.
compareHints: The eastern jack-o'-lantern is the only Omphalotus species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. It's most similar to honey mushrooms in its clustering growth pattern, but honey mushrooms are brown rather than orange and grow with a ring around the stem. The brilliant orange color and bioluminescent gills make jack-o'-lanterns unmistakable once you know what to look for.
